name: AI for Evidence Dossiers and Literature Reviews
blurb: Systematic reviews and value dossiers with language models.
title: AI for Evidence Dossiers and Literature Reviews
answer: Evidence dossiers and systematic reviews depend on finding and screening the literature. In one study a GPT-4 based system reached literature search recall of 71 to 83 percent against 14 to 23 percent for human searchers and screened 1.5 to 2.6 times faster, though results still need expert checking.

reading.body:
In one study a GPT-4 based system found 71 to 83 percent of relevant literature against 14 to 23 percent for human searchers, and screened 1.5 to 2.6 times faster.

That is a recall gap, not a quality claim. The system surfaced more of what was there; it did not judge whether a study was any good. Screening speed and search recall are the two most mechanical steps in a systematic review, and they are the two the study measured. Data extraction and quality appraisal, which carry the actual scientific judgment, are outside what this data covers.

For AI scaling this matters less than it looks. The constraint here is not compute or power but method: assessment bodies accept AI assisted reviews where methods are transparent and results verified, so the AI steps have to be documented as part of the review method and checked by reviewers. The gain is throughput on a slow, labour heavy process, and it is real. The limit is that a dossier still stands on expert verification, and the data says nothing about whether the faster screening changed any final conclusion.

explainer:
Evidence dossiers present the clinical and economic case for a medicine to payers and health technology assessment bodies, and they depend on systematic literature reviews that find and appraise all relevant studies. Systematic reviews are slow: searching databases, screening thousands of records, extracting data and assessing quality.

AI can raise search recall, speed screening and draft data extraction, with published studies showing substantial gains in specific settings. Assessment bodies expect transparent, reproducible methods, so the AI steps must be described as part of the review method, results verified by reviewers, and any limitations reported.

What evidence dossiers are

A dossier assembles everything known about a medicine for a purpose: a regulatory submission, a reimbursement application, a formulary review or a clinical guideline committee. It draws on trials, observational studies, meta analyses, economic models and real world data, and it has to be complete, current and defensible. Building one has meant weeks of searching, screening thousands of abstracts, extracting data into tables and writing a synthesis that a reviewer can trace to its sources.

What AI changes

Language models now handle much of the screening and extraction: deciding which of thousands of records meet inclusion criteria, pulling study characteristics and results into structured tables, and drafting the narrative around them. Systematic review tools report large reductions in screening time, and some can keep a review live by rescreening new publications as they appear. For dossiers that must be refreshed yearly for different countries, that matters.

The standards that still apply

Systematic reviews have published methods standards, and AI does not lower them. Dual screening with a human, documented search strategies, recorded reasons for exclusion and a risk of bias assessment are still expected. Models also miss studies in languages they handle poorly, misread tables, and occasionally invent a citation, so every extracted number is checked against the paper. The practical gain is that people spend their time on judgement and quality rather than on the first pass through the pile.
